title: Antonelli insists Norris ‘deserved to win’ Spanish GP
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has shared his belief that Lando Norris “deserved to win” the Spanish Grand Prix after the reigning World Champion was forced to settle for third – a poorly-timed Virtual Safety Car impacting his chances of victory.

Norris had taken the challenges of the brand-new Madring in his stride as he executed a superb lap to pip Antonelli to pole position, and despite the Italian’s best efforts, he couldn’t find a way past in the opening stint.

He cut two corners in his attempted overtakes and gradually settled into second place behind Norris, who built a confident advantage at the front of the field before disaster struck for McLaren’s strategy.

A Virtual Safety Car was deployed as Lance Stroll came to a halt with brake issues, handing Mercedes the opportunity to change Antonelli’s tyres without losing as much time as they would in normal conditions.

But Norris had already passed the pit entry when the race was neutralised, and by the time he eventually entered for his stop, the VSC period had ended, dropping him from the lead to P5.

Although the Briton managed to recover back to the podium, Antonelli didn’t feel able to fully celebrate his win due to Norris’ misfortune, as he explained: “It was a very difficult race, not straightforward at all, especially trying to manage tyres.

“It’s good to win, but it doesn’t feel as good because I think Lando today deserved to win. But overall, you know, we’ll take it. Other than that, it was a very strong race. I think especially on the hard [tyres] at the end we had really good pace, and now we’re going to keep pushing.”

The 20-year-old also held off Max Verstappen to secure his eighth Grand Prix triumph of the season, which opened up his lead in the Drivers’ Championship to a commanding 81 points over team mate George Russell.

With nine rounds to go, it’s looking increasingly likely that Antonelli could be crowned the sport's youngest-ever World Champion, but he was adamant that the prospect isn’t on his mind.

Asked if he’s able to start thinking about the title, he replied: “That’s exactly what I don’t want to do. I want to keep pushing race by race, you know, keep delivering and keep enjoying all the way, and then trying to do my best every race, and then we’ll see where we end up at the end of the year.”

title: Hamilton explains brake issues that caused Spanish GP DNF
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton believes that Ferrari "had the car to fight for a win" in the Spanish Grand Prix, after the seven-time World Champion was an early retirement with brake problems.

The Briton started fourth for Sunday's 57-lap race at Formula 1's newest venue, the Madring, and made a strong start on the soft Pirelli tyre.

Hamilton initially moved ahead of Max Verstappen's Red Bull on the run to Turn 1 and briefly looked to overtake front row starters Lando Norris and Kimi Antonelli before backing out.

Having been handed third-place back after Verstappen cut the first corner, Hamilton started to encounter braking issues in the opening laps and reported over the radio that he glanced the wall.

Hamilton continued to lose positions over the following laps and ran deep into the Turn 20 run-off area, rejoining the circuit before pulling into the pits and retiring after just seven laps.

"It was already basically before that," Hamilton told Sky F1 when asked if the contact with the wall had caused the braking issue.

"Braking for Turn 5 I hit the brake, the car started stopping and then the pedal took a step and all of a sudden the car didn't de-accelerate as fast a normal.

"I ended up carrying a lot of speed in and just brushed the barrier. After that the pedal came back and then a few corners later, the pedal went long. I don't really know where that's come from."

Hamilton had challenged for pole position on Saturday, while in Sunday's race team mate Charles Leclerc led the most laps as Ferrari tried to keep the Monegasque driver out in the hope of a late Safety Car before finishing fourth.

"We've had a pretty decent car, a good car this weekend and I think we will continue to try and improve it and I think we have better results coming in the future," said Hamilton.

He added: "I think the team’s done an amazing job, so I'm sad for them today that they couldn't get max points. I think we had the car to fight for a win today, and unfortunately it just didn't work out."

title: Antonelli clinches Spanish GP victory over Verstappen and Norris
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has boosted his title ambitions with victory in the Spanish Grand Prix, the Mercedes driver edging out Red Bull’s Max Verstappen and McLaren’s Lando Norris in a race swayed by strategy.

The opening laps saw plenty of clashes up and down the field, with Norris narrowly holding onto the lead from pole position as Antonelli cut two corners during his concerted efforts to pass the Briton.

Antonelli ultimately didn’t need to overtake him on track thanks to a Virtual Safety Car, which played perfectly into Mercedes’ hands but ruined Norris’ chances for victory. A tale of contrasting pit stops unfolded as the Italian gained the net race lead while a slow change dropped Norris behind both Antonelli and Verstappen.

Despite expressing worries with his steering, the 20-year-old inherited control of the race once Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, who didn’t box during the VSC, gave up on his hopes for a Safety Car and finally peeled into the pits after 48 laps.

Adding an eighth win to his season tally, Antonelli has extended his lead to 81 points in the Drivers’ Championship as his team mate George Russell settled for P5, and Lewis Hamilton retired early on due to a issue with his brakes.

Liam Lawson was sixth in the second Red Bull ahead of Franco Colapinto, who made it a successful day for Alpine as their sole scorer, McLaren's Oscar Piastri, Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad and Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg.

Haas’ Esteban Ocon just missed out on points in P11 and was followed by Pierre Gasly and Gabriel Bortoleto, while Yuki Tsunoda took P14 in his third weekend competing for Racing Bulls.

Alex Albon was up next as the lone finisher for Williams, leading Ollie Bearman, local favourite Fernando Alonso and Cadillac’s Valtteri Bottas.

There were four retirements in total – Carlos Sainz failed to complete his home race, Sergio Perez faced a suspected water system issue, and Lance Stroll joined Hamilton in his brake troubles.

AS IT HAPPENED

The Madring had already delivered some of the drama many have come to expect with the debut of a new circuit – Lindblad, Hamilton and Bearman endured shunts across FP2 and FP3, although all bar the Haas man were able to partake in Qualifying.

Hamilton managed to bounce back and claim provisional pole but was quickly outpaced by Antonelli, before McLaren’s Norris completed what he thought was “one of the best laps” of his career to snatch the top spot in style.

Verstappen took a respectable third for Red Bull to lead both Ferrari drivers and the second Mercedes of Russell, who admitted after Qualifying that problems with overheating tyres had limited his performance over the weekend.

He wasn’t the only one concerned about the Pirelli rubber, as previous sessions had shown that graining and thermal degradation could play a significant role in Sunday’s Grand Prix.

As the race start approached at 1500 local time, Haas confirmed that Bearman would start from the pit lane with a new chassis and power unit elements installed following his crash.

Additionally, Stroll and Sainz had grid penalties imposed after Aston Martin fitted engine components to the Canadian’s car to relegate him to P21, just behind Sainz. The stewards concluded that the Williams driver had impeded Cadillac’s Bottas in Q1, dropping him from P17 to P20.

It was revealed that the teams had opted for a wide range of tyre strategies – the front-row starters were on the medium compound, as were Colapinto and Lindblad at the tail end of the top 10.

Verstappen and Hamilton went for the bold option of softs in the hope of making up positions on the opening lap, while Leclerc, Russell, Piastri and Lawson focused on the long game with the white-walled hard tyres.

They were joined by Bortoleto, Gasly, Tsunoda, Alonso, Bottas, Sainz, Stroll and Bearman, whereas Ocon, Albon and Perez chose the mediums. Audi’s Hulkenberg was the only other driver on softs, seemingly targeting an immediate improvement into the points.

As the five red lights went out for the Madring’s inaugural Grand Prix, polesitter Norris came under instant pressure from Antonelli, who took the inside line but was forced to bail out and cut the first chicane. That allowed the McLaren driver to just about cling onto the lead while Antonelli stuck close by.

As another attack followed, the Italian made a near-identical error and went off track once again, giving Verstappen the opportunity to execute a clean overtake at the Bunker to surge into P2.

However, Hamilton wasn’t happy with how the Red Bull driver had stayed ahead at the first corner, insisting that the position needed to be given back. Verstappen, almost simultaneously, reported that Hamilton “almost shunted into me” and was “out of control”, but his complaints didn’t have the intended effect.

His race engineer instructed him to give the spot to Hamilton in order to avoid a possible penalty, and despite a small argument from the Dutchman’s side, he obeyed the order and subsequently let both Antonelli and the Briton through.

To Hamilton’s frustration, the switch didn’t last for long amid his own struggles with the brakes, and he dropped back behind Verstappen and his Ferrari team mate Leclerc. The issue rapidly worsened and he could only watch as his rivals charged past, with the Scuderia deciding to retire the car just seven laps in.

With Hamilton out of contention, Norris had steadily built his lead to 4.5s over Antonelli, aided by the Italian suffering an off-track moment that cost him a chunk of time. The closest battle at this stage was between Colapinto and Lawson for P6, both drivers having fought past McLaren’s Piastri when the Australian made contact with Russell on the opening lap.

Elsewhere, Russell had clearly spent some time revising his tyre management overnight, suggesting to the team that they could try an alternative strategy to get past Leclerc, who was running in P4 just ahead of the Briton.

A check-in on the grid’s two Spaniards showed that their home crowd had little to celebrate – not only was a top-10 finish a distant prospect, but they also came to blows at Turn 5, with Alonso adamant that Sainz had squeezed him into the wall. The stewards agreed with his view, later handing the Williams driver a five-second penalty for the collision.

Meanwhile, Norris’ advantage at the front continued to increase, and he received further encouragement when the team informed him that Antonelli’s medium tyres weren’t coping with the high-grip asphalt as well as his, implying that he might try to extend his opening stint.

That approach soon fell apart when Aston Martin’s Stroll came to a halt at Turn 20, marking the second retirement of the day caused by brake problems. The Virtual Safety Car was deployed, handing Mercedes and Red Bull the perfect opportunity to call Antonelli, Russell and Verstappen into the pits.

The mandatory reduced speeds only lasted as long as it took to bring Stroll’s car behind the barrier, meaning that Norris ran out of time to take advantage and only stopped once normal racing conditions resumed.

Adding insult to injury, it was an agonisingly slow tyre change that kept him stationary for 7s and he eventually emerged in P5 behind Leclerc – who hadn’t pitted – Antonelli, Verstappen and Russell.

With the sole Ferrari driver now leading, Antonelli initially closed the gap before falling further back, stating that “the steering wheel feels weird”. Mercedes couldn’t find any reason why in their data, but did warn him that any further track limit violations could result in a time penalty.

Over half the race distance down, Norris was giving it his all to recover from the disastrous timing of the Virtual Safety Car as he battled to get past Russell, which was made much easier when the latter was brought in for a second stop.

Ferrari were on a considerably different strategy as they continued to keep Leclerc out, hanging their hopes of a podium finish on the chance of a Safety Car or red flag. Antonelli consistently remained around 2s adrift and led Verstappen and Norris, who spent multiple laps searching for a way past the Dutchman.

Further back, a thrilling contest occurred between eighth-placed Bortoleto, Colapinto, Piastri in the second McLaren, who had been knocked back early on with a damaged front wing, and Racing Bulls’ Lindblad.

Battling for the final few spots in the top 10, the group nearly came together as the race entered the last 10 laps, but a similar fight was also developing at the front between Antonelli, Verstappen and Norris.

Leclerc was called into the pits at the end of Lap 48, releasing the trio to decide who would claim the honour of winning the Spanish Grand Prix.

That was the ideal time for Antonelli to pick up the pace as he left Verstappen in the clutches of Norris, who had the best opportunity to improve to P2 when the Dutchman cut Turn 5. The reigning World Champion drew alongside but couldn’t make a move stick, remaining in third place as the chequered flag fell.

Antonelli won with a comfortable margin of 4.2s over his nearest rivals, with Leclerc and Russell much further behind in P4 and P5 respectively. Lawson finished a respectable sixth in his third weekend substituting Isack Hadjar at Red Bull, leading Colapinto, Piastri, Lindblad and Hulkenberg.

Ocon was next as Haas failed to score for the ninth time this season, with the Frenchman taking P11 ahead of Gasly, Bortoleto and Tsunoda. P15 belonged to Albon, who was followed over the line by Bearman, Alonso and Bottas.

Ferrari’s Hamilton wasn’t the only one hampered by his brakes as Aston Martin’s Stroll retired for the same reason, while Sainz and Perez also didn’t finish the Spanish Grand Prix due to separate issues with their cars.

Key quote

"It was a very difficult race, not straightforward at all, especially trying to manage tyres," Antonelli said. "It’s good to win, but it doesn’t feel as good because I think Lando today deserved to win. But overall, you know, we’ll take it. And other than that, it was a very strong race. I think especially on the hard at the end we had really good pace, and yeah, now we’re gonna keep pushing."

What's next

title: Beganovic dominates F2 Feature Race at the Madring
excerpt:
Dino Beganovic was untouchable as he claimed a lights-to-flag victory in the Madrid F2 Feature Race.

The DAMS Lucas Oil driver made an excellent start from pole position and managed two Safety Car restarts perfectly before claiming his first win of the season.

Beganovic won by more than seven seconds over Rodin Motorsport’s Alexander Dunne, as Hitech’s Ritomo Miyata followed up his Sprint Race victory with a run to P3 in the Feature.

Invicta Racing’s Joshua Duerksen finished fourth ahead of AIX Racing’s Emerson Fittipaldi and ART Grand Prix driver Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak.

MP Motorsport’s Gabriele Minì made several eye-catching overtakes on his way to finishing P7 after starting 13th, with Rodin’s Martinius Stenshorne following him home.

Roman Bilinski took the chequered flag in P10 but gained a position once Rafael Camara’s 10-second time penalty – for causing a collision with Ollie Goethe – was applied.

The Invicta Racing driver did do enough to finish in P10 and score one point, while championship leader Nikola Tsolov ended up at the back after contact.

The Formula 2 drivers will hit the track once again in Baku for Round 12 from September 24-26.

title: OFFICIAL GRID: Who starts where for the Spanish GP
excerpt:
A spectacular Qualifying session around the equally spectacular Madring circuit will see the Spanish Grand Prix start with reigning World Champion Lando Norris on pole for McLaren, and the Mercedes of championship leader Kimi Antonelli alongside.

Firmly in the mix as always when the lights go out will be Max Verstappen, the Dutchman starting third in the Red Bull ahead of the Ferraris of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc. Then come the second Mercedes and McLaren cars of George Russell and Oscar Piastri.

Red Bull stand-in Liam Lawson is a creditable eighth on the grid, while arguably the biggest surprise in the top 10 is Franco Colapinto, the Argentine driver having out-qualified Alpine team mate – and polesitter last time out – Pierre Gasly by a full five places.

Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad recovered well from his Friday crash to make Q3 and lines up tenth. Less fortunate was fellow Briton Ollie Bearman, whose heavy contact with the Madrid barriers in FP3 meant his Haas was not ready for Qualifying. He will start from the pit lane with a new chassis and power unit elements.

Like Bearman, Lance Stroll did not set a lap time – and following several new power unit elements being fitted to his Aston Martin, the Canadian will start from the back of the grid.

The only man to take a driving-related grid penalty is Williams' Carlos Sainz, who's dropped three places from his original P17 qualifying position for impeding Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas during the Saturday session.

title: Ugochukwu is crowned champion as Taponen earns maiden F3 win
excerpt:
Ugo Ugochukwu has won the F3 Drivers’ Championship, taking the title in the final race of the season in Madrid to beat Freddie Slater to the crown.

Ugochukwu finished P2 on the road to become the first F3 Champion from the United States, while Tuukka Taponen became the first Finnish driver to win an F3 race as he secured top spot in Feature Race 2 on Sunday.

Taponen was able to hold the lead into Turn 1 from pole position, the first driver to do so all weekend around the Madring.

From there, the MP Motorsport driver controlled the gap to Ugochukwu behind, with the Campos Racing car staying within touching distance and DRS range throughout.

A late-race Safety Car set up a final lap sprint to the finish, but Taponen remained calm and collected to take his first F3 victory in the final race of the 2026 season.

The result means Ugochukwu is the 2026 FIA Formula 3 Drivers' Champion, finishing on 159 points. Slater winds up second in the standings on 145 points. Taponen's win lifts the Finn up to third in the Championship.

Entering the day level on points with Slater and starting from P2, the Campos driver kept himself out of trouble to earn a podium to complete a turnaround, having trailed the Briton in the points coming into this weekend.

Pedro Clerot was on the podium once again in Madrid after taking his first F3 victory in Feature Race 1 on Saturday, rounding out the rostrum in third position for Rodin Motorsport.

Slater, the TRIDENT and Audi Development Driver, finished where he started in eighth position, leaving him second in the points after a season-long battle.

title: Norris in title fight 'until it's not possible' – Brown
excerpt:
Zak Brown believes Lando Norris is still in contention for this year's drivers' title after claiming pole position for the Spanish Grand Prix, stating "until it's not possible, it's possible".

Norris claimed pole position for Sunday's inaugural race at the Madring, but was left "shocked" at the result having nearly collided with the wall at the final corner after running slightly wide.

The result was even more surprising as Norris missed nearly all running in Friday's Free Practice 2 with a gearbox issue, before claiming top spot on Saturday.

After a sluggish start under the new-for-2026 regulations, McLaren and Norris have hit their stride this season, with the reining world champions having taken back-to-back wins in Hungary and the Netherlands.

The gap to Kimi Antonelli, who leads the drivers' standings, sits at 96 points with 10 Grands Prix remaining this season.

Max Verstappen overturned a 104-point gap to Norris' team mate Oscar Piastri last season, with McLaren team boss Brown believing such a feat could be possible again.

"It's definitely possible I think. I can only speak for McLaren, until it's not possible, it's possible," he told F1 TV post-Qualifying ahead of Sunday's 57-lap race.

"Obviously you have to be realistic but anything can happen. Today's F1 at the moment with reliability, the new power units are a little less predictable than the last generation. Anything can happen. All we can do is go for the wins every weekend and see if we can close the gap."

The inaugural race at the Madring is expected to be a tight tactical battle, with overtaking difficult on the high-speed circuit, while tyre degradation is likely to be high with hot temperatures.

Brown believes that Antonelli may have one eye on securing points in his quest for a maiden F1 title during his sophomore season, but is not expecting an easy race for victory.

"I think he wants to win, we want to win. I think Kimi is racing for a championship and Lando is racing for a championship," added Brown.

"The way he's going to get there, he's got to win. I think they'll do what they do. He'll be aggressive, it'll be interesting to see how the race plays out.

"It's been remarkably calm so far for what I think potentially can happen here with the walls.

"Difficult to pass, so we just need a clean start and then it's a long pit lane, so we'll see how strategy plays out.

"Very proud of what the team has been able to do on improving a car over the course of a weekend, because I think on Friday we wouldn't have predicted pole."

title: Lewis Hamilton explains cause of first Ferrari retirement in 10 months
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has explained the sequence of events behind his brake failure that led to his retirement from the Spanish Grand Prix.

Hamilton retired on Lap 7 of 57 in Madrid after the SF-26 machine suffered a brake failure, with Hamilton going off at Turn 20 as he struggled to slow the Ferrari down after early battles with Max Verstappen.

Hamilton had been the only driver to complete every grand prix and Sprint race lap in 2026 prior to the retirement, which is his first since the 2025 Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

It is the first time since the 2014 Canadian Grand Prix that Hamilton has suffered a brakes-related retirement, and is the 35th retirement of his career in his 394th start.

"I had a good start, I didn't see Max, and I wasn't in the battle going down to Turn 5," Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365.

"But then I went into Turn 5, I hit the brake, and it started stopping okay, and then the pedal took a step, and it wouldn't stop all of a sudden.

"I ended up going wide, and that's when I tapped the barrier, but it didn't really feel bad, like a bad touch.

"Then the pedal came back, and it was fine for the next corners, and things were looking okay, and then the pedal went long."

The article continues below.

Hamilton addresses Verstappen battle

As for Verstappen's complaints about the move at Turn 1, when presented with what the Red Bull driver had said, Hamilton offered a short reply.

"Well, I thought it was pretty good racing, to be honest," the Ferrari driver replied.

title: Max Verstappen issues comical response to successful Lando Norris defence
excerpt:
Max Verstappen issued a comical response when asked how he successfully kept Lando Norris behind him in the closing laps of the Spanish Grand Prix, held at the Madring.

The Dutchman started from third but gained a position to secure an impressive second-place finish, more than was expected of Red Bull heading into the event.

It was an eventful start for Verstappen, who cut the opening corner, passing Lewis Hamilton and race winner Kimi Antonelli in the process.

Red Bull instructed Verstappen to return both positions, something the four-time world champion did after initially complaining.

Hamilton's retirement promoted the 28-year-old back into third, before he rose to second after Norris was unable to pit during a virtual safety car period while leading the race. Verstappen did pit.

Fresher tyres allowed Norris to catch Verstappen in the closing laps, yet the reigning world champion was unable to find a way past.

"Looking at the race pace, for us, a great result," said Verstappen.

"Lando got unlucky with the VSC, so for us P2 is an incredible result because you could see how much he was catching me but around here you can't pass, so I could keep him behind."

Verstappen Madring criticism continues after strong podium

Verstappen has been critical of the Madring's layout throughout the weekend, mostly because it does not feature an overtaking opportunity.

That, in itself, made defending simple for Red Bull's star driver.

Asked how he kept Norris behind, Verstappen explained: "Just keep the car in the middle.

"That works quite well around here and just trying to keep the grip in the tyres, which was the hardest part of that stint."

title: Lando Norris laments rotten Spanish GP luck: 'Nothing I could do'
excerpt:
Lando Norris conceded there was nothing he could do and that luck was not on his side after missing out on victory in the Spanish Grand Prix.

From a "masterpiece" of a pole position at the Madring, a word used by McLaren team principal Andrea Stella to describe his driver's out-of-nowhere lap, Norris comfortably led the opening 14 laps.

However, an incident involving Aston Martin's Lance Stroll sparked a virtual safety car. Unfortunately for Norris, he missed the window by five seconds, whilst behind him, Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and Red Bull's Max Verstappen both pitted.

Norris then pitted just as the VSC, coming out fifth behind leader Charles Leclerc in his Ferrari, Antonelli, Verstappen and the second Mercedes of George Russell.

After Mercedes opted to pit Russell for a second time, and Leclerc pitted late on, Norris moved up to third, and despite hounding Verstappen over the closing laps, around a track where it proved almost impossible to pass, the Briton had to settle for third as Antonelli took the chequered flag.

Assessing the timing of the VSC, speaking to Sky Sports F1, Norris said: "There was nothing I could do.

"Congrats to Kimi. Luck was not on our side. I gave it a good fight to try and catch up to Max, but difficult to pass. He didn't make any mistakes...yeah, a tough race. One that got away from us.

"I felt like we deserved it, but that's racing sometimes. We'll take it on the chin and try again next time."

[Article continues below]

'More wins possible' - Norris

As to what McLaren can achieve over the coming grands prix through to the end of the season, Norris added: "Tough to know. These things don't come easy. I do feel like I'm working hard, getting a lot out of the car.

"Yesterday was pretty phenomenal to get pole, and I drove a perfect race today, but luck wasn't with me.

"We'll keep it up; the team is doing an amazing job, and we're working hard. We have to continue to work hard because these guys are doing an amazing job, and it's tough at the top.

"We'll keep pushing, keep trying. More wins are possible, so we'll keep our heads up and keep pushing."

title: Kimi Antonelli makes Lando Norris concession after fortunate Spanish victory
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has conceded that Lando Norris deserved to win the Spanish Grand Prix, but declared "we'll take it" after a fortunate virtual safety car.

Antonelli now holds an 81-point advantage over George Russell, who finished in fifth place following his eighth win of the season.

It means Antonelli is likely to be leading the championship by the time F1 arrives in Austin for the United States Grand Prix, with 83 points on offer across the Azerbaijan-Bahrain-Singapore races, with Singapore being a Sprint.

Antonelli's win came after he was able to pit behind a virtual safety car for Lance Stroll's stopped Aston Martin, with leader Norris having just missed the pit entry under the VSC conditions.

By the time Norris pitted, the race had resumed under green flag conditions, meaning Antonelli and Max Verstappen were able to get ahead.

In the end, Antonelli won by 4.3s from Verstappen with Norris in third, and beat Russell by 29.8s as he took a giant leap towards becoming the youngest world champion in F1 history.

Reflecting after the record-equalling 251st win for a Mercedes engine, Antonelli made clear that he felt Norris was the best driver on the day.

"It was a very difficult race, not straightforward at all, especially trying to manage tyres, but I think today it is good to win, but it doesn't feel as good because I think Lando today deserved the win," Antonelli said.

"But overall we'll take it. And other than that, it was a very strong race. I think, especially on the hard at the end, we had really good pace.

"Now we're going to keep pushing. I want to keep pushing race by race, keep delivering and keep enjoying it all the way, and I'm trying to do my best every race, and then we'll see where we end up at the end of the year."

title: Kimi Antonelli delivers latest F1 title blow as Lewis Hamilton suffers brake failure at Spanish GP
excerpt:
Victory number eight of the season for Kimi Antonelli, who has further extended his championship lead!

Kimi Antonelli has won the Spanish Grand Prix, taking his eighth victory of the 2026 F1 campaign.

The Mercedes driver has further extended his championship advantage, crossing the line ahead of Max Verstappen and Lando Norris.

It was a disastrous race for seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton, who was forced to retire his car early on after suffering a brake failure.

His team-mate Charles Leclerc led for much of the race after staying out under a virtual safety car, but was forced to concede the lead to Antonelli late on.

Kimi Antonelli delivers latest F1 title blow as Lewis Hamilton suffers brake failure at Spanish GP

# Driver Team Time Tyre

Results are being loaded...

Norris maintains early control

On the opening lap, Norris held onto the lead while Antonelli attacked, running off the track on two occasions while doing so.

As a result, he was forced to give up his position to Norris, having moved ahead off the circuit - but as he did so, Verstappen managed to slip through.

But Verstappen himself was asked to give his place back to Hamilton, forcing the Dutchman to lose two positions as he also had to allow Antonelli through in the process.

Soon after, though, Hamilton’s race would come completely undone, as a brake issue forced him to retire from the grand prix.

Up front, Norris stretched out his lead across the opening 10 laps, pulling himself well clear of Antonelli.

However, the race would soon be turned on its head, as Lance Stroll also noted brake issues of his own, which saw him end the race in the wall.

© XPBimages

Virtual safety car results in McLaren pain

A virtual safety car was then called, which saw much of the field come in for a pit stop.

Unfortunately for Norris, it was called right after he passed the pit lane entry, allowing Antonelli and the rest to get a cheap pit stop.

Norris pitted the next time around, but at that stage the virtual safety car had ended, which dropped Norris to fifth place after his stop.

To add insult to injury, he suffered a slow stop - ensuring he rejoined behind Leclerc, Antonelli, Verstappen and Russell.

Leclerc was the only driver in the front-running pack who did not elect to take a pit stop under the virtual safety car as Ferrari targeted a one-stop strategy.

Norris was able to gain a position when Russell pitted on lap 29 and spent the next handul of laps closing in on Verstappen for third.

Grand Prix

Spanish GP

Run to the flag

With Antonelli held up out front by Leclerc, Verstappen and Norris closed in before he was released into clear air when the Ferrari pitted on lap 49.

From there, he was able to eke out the gap and seal the victory.

Verstappen came under significant pressure from Norris in the final laps, however, the Dutchman held on to take the runner-up spot.

Leclerc had to settle for fourth place, while Russell took sixth on the road in the second Mercedes.

After a disappointing outing last time out in Italy, Liam Lawson returned to the points - albeit in a rather lonely sixth place.

Franco Colapinto consolidated another strong result with a run to seventh place, leading Oscar Piastri across the line, who suffered another turbulent race for McLaren.

Arvid Lindblad's positive rookie campaign continued with another point-scoring result in ninth after he held off Nico Hulkenberg in the final laps.

F1 will return in two weeks' time with the Azerbaijan Grand Prix from Baku.

title: Max Verstappen fumes after being handed Spanish GP order
excerpt:
Max Verstappen was left fuming in the cockpit of his Red Bull after being ordered to give positions back at the start of the Spanish Grand Prix.

From third on the grid, Verstappen tussled with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton into Turn 1 at the new Madring circuit, forcing the four-time F1 champion off the track through Turn 2.

As the lap continued, Verstappen managed to nestle into second behind race leader Lando Norris in his McLaren after the Dutchman passed championship leader Kimi Antonelli in his Mercedes.

After Hamilton complained over the radio that Verstappen should give the position back, Verstappen outlined his case, making clear he and the seven-time F1 champion would have collided if he had stayed on track.

As the first few laps unfolded, Verstappen was eventually told by race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase to give up his second place.

Over the radio, an angry Verstappen said: "Mate, what the f*** are you guys talking about? He would've shunted it.

"Like, what are you guys talking about? If I just stay on the track, I am out of the race."

Shortly after that message, Verstappen eventually relented, giving up his second position as Antonelli and then Hamilton passed him, dropping to fourth.

Verstappen soon regained a position, however, due to Hamilton eventually retiring with a brake failure.

title: Lewis Hamilton suffers huge title blow with early Spanish GP retirement
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton's hopes of winning the 2026 F1 championship appear virtually over after an early retirement on Lap 7 of the Spanish GP.

From fourth on the grid, Hamilton battled with Red Bull's Max Verstappen on the opening lap, but after being waved passed after the Dutchman was told to give the place back, Hamilton's Ferrari started to develop brake problems.

He first cut the Turns 5 and 6 chicane, before then locking up and going off at Turn 20, and dropping down the order.

He reported in that he had "no brakes" and retired on Lap 7 of 57.

Hamilton now loses his record as the only driver to complete every race and Sprint lap in 2026, and it is his first brake-related DNF since the 2014 Canadian Grand Prix for Mercedes.

He was 76 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli heading into the race, with the Italian currently running second, worth 18 points, behind race leader Lando Norris, with Verstappen third, the sole remaining Ferrari of Charles Leclerc in fourth, and George Russell in fifth.

title: Kimi Antonelli hopeful of solution after painful Madring experience
excerpt:
The suspicion is there will be many a repeat of what Kimi Antonelli experienced in practice.

Kimi Antonelli is hopeful of a solution to avoid a 'painful' repeat of his experience in practice ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix.

Antonelli will start the race from second on the grid at the Madring after being beaten to pole by McLaren's Lando Norris by 0.011s. Max Verstappen lines up third in his Red Bull, with Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc fourth and fifth for Ferrari.

With overtaking expected to be at a premium at the circuit, teams and drivers will have to find alternative methods to make gains on track. Mercedes driver Antonelli feels tyre management will offer one route forward.

Assessing the challenge of the new track, Antonelli said: "I think Monaco is probably still a bit more intense, but this track also takes quite a bit of effort to try and put the lap together.

"And overtaking, yes, I think it's going to be very difficult. In practice, I spent two laps behind a Williams trying to painfully get past - just really difficult, especially because the deg is quite big and when you're behind you start sliding more. It just makes your life a bit tougher."

[Article continues below]

Antonelli keen to put Norris under pressure

Should Antonelli find himself behind Norris at the start, he feels there may be a way he will be able to work his way past the F1 champion.

"The only thing you can do is try to put pressure on the car in front, try to make them make a mistake or make them deg a bit more, and then you try to play with strategy," he said. "But when you have a very similar pace, it is difficult to make a move."

The 20-year-old, who leads team-mate George Russell by 66 points going into the race, expects it to be decided by tyre life.

"The race is going to be a lot about managing the tyres and not deg-ing off so much as well," he said.

"We don't really know how the hard tyre is, how resilient it is, so we may have two stops, three stops. We'll see.

"But the key, especially in that first stint, will be to try and manage as much as you know without giving up too much time, trying to manage the tyres."

title: 2026 Spanish Grand Prix - F2 Madrid Feature Race results
excerpt:
Dino Beganovic won a frenetic and highly entertaining F2 feature race at the Madring, beating Alex Dunne by seven seconds ahead of the 2026 F1 Spanish Grand Prix.

A mid-race safety car afforded the two drivers, who started together on the front row, and Ritomo Miyata, who finished third, a cheap pit stop.

This helped them hold off the charge of the offset strategy runners, led by Mari Boya, who pitted early after the first safety car interruption and had significantly closed the gap to the leaders.

Kush Maini crashed in the opening laps, which triggered the initial disruption, and championship contender Rafael Camara pushed Oliver Goethe into the wall on the outside of Turn 2 to instigate the second, for which he was handed a 10-second time penalty, which dropped him from ninth to tenth at the chequered flag.

Prior to that, he was involved in a spirited fight with Boya and standings leader Nikola Tsolov, who tumbled down the order at the end, as they attempted to work their way past Goethe.

Initially, Tsolov made a move up into Turn 5 to head that train, but he missed the chicane and needed to hand the places back.

That opened the door for Camara, who stuck his car around the outside, slightly damaging the front wing of his title rival.

Due to the stoppages, it became a time-limited race. However, full points have been awarded for the result as 31 of 32 scheduled laps were completed.

Colton Herta, who continued to feel unwell and was withdrawn from the sprint, also did not take part in the feature race.

title: F1 teams weighing up Madrid gamble as key decision awaits
excerpt:
The Madring Circuit is the new home of the Spanish Grand Prix, and the debut race will have teams thinking about their approach.

Lando Norris will lead the field away for the start of the Spanish Grand Prix on Sunday, held around the all-new Madring circuit.

The reigning champion narrowly bested Kimi Antonelli to the fastest lap in Q3, taking his third pole position in four rounds.

Having won his last two races from pole position, Norris is seeking his third victory of the year and become the first driver to win a race at the Madring Circuit.

However, a crucial decision awaits the teams as they weigh up the possibility of a one-stop versus a two-stop strategy.

Pirelli has indicated that a one-stop strategy is set to be the most likely route to success, with a medium-hard option on the table.

It also indicated that a soft-hard option is available, which would offer drivers more grip at the start to gain track position, but would result in an earlier drop-off in pace.

Grand Prix

Spanish GP

Pirelli confirm two-stop race an option

However, teams could also elect to run a two-stop strategy, which would likely see drivers start on the medium compound before two stints on the hard.

With high temperatures forecast for the race, it's possible that teams may be forced into the two-stopper if tyre wear proves too much to bear.

However, it would be a gamble as it would likely put the driver into traffic, and if the junior categories are anything to go by this weekend in Madrid, overtaking will be a significant challenge.

Another factor that the teams will need to consider is the length of the pit lane, which is among the longest on the calendar.

Drivers are expected to lose around 24 seconds through the pit lane, making an extra stop less attractive.

But with the barriers not far away around the track, the chance of a safety car is higher than at traditional circuits and has no doubt played a part in the calculations from the teams.
